title: Conversations With the Buddha and Our Mind
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The teacher encourages us to approach life and conversations with an open mind and heart, rather than trying to control or manage our thoughts. This means being willing to step into uncertainty and embracing the changes that arise, much like a conversation unfolds naturally. By doing so, we can cultivate courage, love, and non-attachment, which are key to liberation from wrong views and finding freedom in the present moment.

sentences.text: Good morning everybody.
I feel not as connected to you guys this retreat.
Anyway, I've been thinking about you.
The Dokusan room turns out doesn't really have Wi-Fi, so it's hard to connect in Dokusan.
So what can you do?
Can you hear me okay like this?
Okay.
All right.
You guys can hear?
Okay.
I was appreciating earlier, I was looking at the job sheet, the little job sheet of who does what job.
The job sheets that I originally saw, when I was practicing when I was younger, at Green Gulch and Tassajara, would list all the positions, the tanto in the Kokyo, the servers and so on.
They wouldn't normally list the teacher, because everybody knows, why would you need to write that down?
When we first started making those job sheets here, I just had this impulse: it'll be good to put the teacher on there.
Just to see and remember that it's just another job, right?
Like everything else, it rotates, it just rotates on a little different schedule.
And like everything else, it's not like we seek a five-star Michelin chef to be Tenzo and we seek a world-class musician to be Doan or anything like that.
We seek a willing Dharma practitioner with a good heart, who probably is going to make lots of mistakes, who has to learn by doing like we all do, and will serve the sangha.
One of the things I always have loved about this form is that we also have this idea of equanimity, of evenness.
So we appreciate everybody equally, everybody contributes.
Even if you're not on the job sheet, you contribute so much through your presence, through your practice, through your logging in, it turns out we didn't know that then.
So all that to say, I'm feeling lately a little more that way than like I have anything special.
I feel like somebody has put me on the sheet, so I'm giving the talk.
I hope that's okay.
I'll do my best to ring the bell at the right time.
And luckily, if you say the wrong thing in the talk or ring the bell at the wrong time, it actually doesn't matter that much, or it turns out to be beneficial.
A little not too long ago I found out that I said something years ago that really made somebody angry, and that turned out to be really useful to them.
So what can we do in this human life but have a conversation, really?
Isn't this whole thing just a conversation?
Were you appreciating the way Cathy noticed with us yesterday that the whole Diamond Sutra is like one long conversation?
We're more like eavesdroppers than anybody being told anything, right?
We just happen to be there listening as the Buddha and Subhuti had a long conversation.
But it's not a conversation without some context, right?
Chapter one does lay out the scene.
The monks are in their daily life of practice.
They go out to do their begging round, presumably after they've done their morning meditation, starting early.
They settle down and have their meal and the Buddha gets all settled in.
He washes his feet, maybe somebody washes his feet with him.
And don't forget that a couple of the 32 marks are on his feet.
So that must have been really moving, to help wash the Buddha's feet and see these Dharma wheels on his feet.
Like, wow.

The implication with all these Mahayana Sutras, well, I guess all the Sutras, is that the Buddha probably would have been content to just sit there in silence, enjoy the afternoon, the weather, the breath, but somebody had a question.
And so a conversation out loud began, and the Buddha asked that question.
I appreciate that question, particularly because when we're sitting for days, like we have been to different extents, aren't we in a long conversation with our thinking mind, amongst other things?
The thinking mind often has a lot to say.

We may zip around trying to decide if we are our thinking mind or if we're somebody else or if we're a second layer that's watching and listening and trying to straighten it out or shut it up or encourage it or something.
So it's interesting to notice that the question the Buddha actually asked was specifically about that.
Did you notice that?
He asked, how do I control my thinking?
How do we work with our thinking?
As noble sons and daughters, blah, blah, blah.
There was a whole lot of language around it, but he was really asking how we be with our thinking.
I looked at a few different translations and it seems pretty consistent that he said some version of how do I manage or control my thinking.
Thich Nhat Hanh has "mastered our thinking."
Red Pine has "control our thinking."
Another helpful commentator is a Korean American monk named Mu Song, maybe he's Korean.
He has "keep our thoughts under control."
This is kind of strange because it doesn't seem to mesh with the instructions, does it?
Did you notice that back when we did chapter two?
The instructions we receive are more like: let thoughts come and go, don't be attached to them, let them flow like rivers, let them flow across the vast blue sky of the mind like clouds.
This doesn't sound like what we usually mean when we say control.
It's very open.
A thousand years later, Dogen's telling us think not thinking.
So that's not exactly control.
But there's a sense here of some kind of active engagement, right?
Not just checking out and letting the thoughts do what they may.
I've been trying to think about this, probably a mistake, but I have been.

I was also appreciating Hannah's appreciation that she expressed with us the other day about Zazen itself, and how the conversation we have with Zazen, through Zazen, does usually have a different quality to it when we do it for a longer time, for a whole day or for days.
It's such a rich, I forget how she said it, but such a rich engagement, right?
Such a rich conversation with our minds and hearts when we are longer in Zazen.
Because everything under the sun comes up: peaceful, exasperating, monotonous, surprising, inspiring.
And much of the time we're not even really knowing what's going on, right?
If we're honest, what's happening?
I'm in a conversation, but I'm not sure what the language is.
Or who's here?
Am I here?
What's me?
And the Diamond Sutra reminds us to be curious about this idea of me, right?
That's what it feels like.
And that's what they mean in there by lifespan.
What's this mean?
So it's a really interesting practice we have received, and it must attract us enough that we're still here.
The instructions seem to be contradictory or lacking.
And half the time, maybe most of the time, we don't really know what we're doing.
And somehow that's just right.
Isn't that weird?
Somehow that's just right.
It's just what we need.
Maybe because it accurately mirrors our actual life, that we don't know what we're doing most of the time.
And it's all a conversation.
It's constantly changing.
We suffer and get confused sometimes from the changes, but we sometimes accept the changes and then we feel good and even appreciate the changes, like any conversation.

So it is curious that an aspect of our conditioning that leads to suffering, that the Buddha talked about from the get-go, is that there's this part of us that desires it to be sort of steady and static and predictable.
But what conversation would that be?
Would that just be repeating something back and forth with your friend forever?
It wouldn't be very good.
So maybe Zazen and our practice reveal to us that we have a messed up expectation and that the actual conversation is much richer, more varied and more beautiful than anything we could have imagined.

I think Cathy said this, or maybe I thought it when she was speaking, but she also mentioned that the conversation in the Diamond Sutra is a courageous conversation, like a willingness to dig in to not knowing, as she did say.
So that's really letting the conversation go where it's going to go, isn't it?
We don't know where it's going to go.
Thinking about just ordinary conversations between us, isn't it true that we sometimes go into a conversation with somebody thinking we know what they're going to say?
How limiting that is, right?
How flat that is.
There's a certain comfort in it because we think we have control, back to control.
But it's not a real conversation.
In a real conversation, we don't know where it's going to go.
And that requires courage.

So I love this thought that we're eavesdropping and being moved, confused, inspired and annoyed by a long conversation, a long courageous conversation between Subhuti and the Buddha, witnessed by all the assembly, including us.
I've always loved the word courage a lot more.
First, I thought of courage as just this kind of aggressive feeling, like a military thing.
Through the breach, over the wall, right?
That's a certain kind of courage.
Very aggressive.
But then some years ago, I learned that the etymology of courage is really moving.
It comes from old French for having heart.
So courage actually means heart, actually means heartfulness.
So a heartful conversation.
I have a Ukrainian friend named Janina, Janina Scarlett.
For some reason it came to me that I want to share with you a conversation I had with her some years ago.
It feels good also to honor Janina as a part of this conversation about Ukraine and Russia and all that's going on, and to send her love in that way, too.
Janina Scarlett was born in the Ukraine in 1983, in a region of Ukraine with a name we all are probably familiar with: Chernobyl.

In 1986, when she was three years old, the Chernobyl nuclear reactors melted down, as you know, spraying radiation for hundreds of miles and very intensely in that region, which is still to this day mostly uninhabitable.
It's hard to get your mind around that kind of conversation we could be having with a place.
Janina and her family were strongly affected, and her especially.
She had severe migraines and seizures throughout her upbringing.
In adulthood, they finally started to diminish.
To make things even more challenging for Janina and her family, they're Jewish.

I don't know if it was that area or Ukraine in general, but there was a lot of anti-Semitism in the 80s and 90s in Ukraine or around there, which obviously must be a more rich and complicated conversation since President Zelensky is Jewish himself, so that's interesting.
But it was oppressive enough and scary enough, plus the meltdown, that they immigrated to the U.S. when she was about 12.
With Janina's limited English and her poor health, she was teased and bullied in school.
She was also very small.
Somehow word got out that she was also a victim of the Chernobyl nuclear disaster, and so the kids called her radioactive and stayed away from her at school.
Meanwhile, like so many immigrants do, she was supplementing her English learning a lot with American music and American TV.
She got especially into the X-Men, the TV show based on comic books, one of the first successful ones by Marvel.
From there, she got super into superheroes and they were her comfort.
Her favorite character in the X-Men was Storm.
I don't really know X-Men, but I looked it up and Storm is a female character with special powers, and she kind of mutated like the other X-Men characters due to stress and suffering.
It caused her to become a different type of being through her suffering and terrible trauma.
Storm's own particular power is that she can control the weather.
That's why her name.
But the great thing about superheroes is they have both great powers and great weaknesses, right?
Great sufferings too.

So Janina really took refuge in her comic book heroes, a frame of reference for understanding difficult feelings and a pathway to courage, a way to go forward in this world where she felt so different from everybody else.
She's intellectually smart and she got through school and maybe took refuge in being a good student, probably.
She went on to become a therapist, a psychotherapist.
Like most new professionals, she did her best to learn how to do it right and follow the rules and fit in.
When you join a new profession, you start there usually if you're going to last.
She was doing that as a young adult into her 30s.
That's when I met her in 2012.
She and I really connected.
I'm not sure why.
We were in this big intensive training, 50 students, put on by a group out of Stanford University around teaching compassion.
They developed a course based on Tibetan Buddhism, and there's a prominent Tibetan Buddhist involved in this, a really sweet guy.
But anyway, she and I somehow really connected, even though she was very quiet and very shy, hardly said anything.
We ended up going on long walks when I'd go down to these trainings.

At some point she shared with me, admitted her secret, which is that she's a total superhero geek, comic book geek, and that she loves all that world, but she felt a need to keep that hidden so people would take her seriously.
And she had an idea.
Her idea was that since superheroes helped her so much in her own healing, maybe they could help other people she was working with as a therapist.

Particularly she was working with veterans then at the Veterans Administration Hospital in San Diego, and she shared with me what I also learned when I got to work with veterans: there's so much suffering there, as you'd expect, and so much strength, too.
Superheroes, for sure.

She had this idea that it could really help to encourage them to think about who their favorite superhero might be, to feel the strength of that superhero, and also to relate to their challenge and their so-called weakness and their vulnerability.
Superman never knows when the kryptonite's going to come out.
Peter Parker never knows if he's ever going to be at peace with being Spider-Man, like what happened to me, you know?
And not just classic superheroes.
Maybe people might relate to the characters in Harry Potter or Star Trek, and that could really help them heal.
What would Hermione Granger do?
Logic and reason are powerful and can take you far, but what does Spock do when his emotions overcome him?
What do you do?
So she told me about all this and I shared a little bit about a challenge I was feeling in a similar way.
I had just started the Mindfulness Northwest organization.
It was pretty much just me and a few friends part time, and we were also bickering, my friends and I.
I had received a certain sort of mandate that I could offer just this one class I had been taught, but I was interested in the idea of creating other classes that fit the situations I was in better.
It's a long story.
Maybe I could even devise a way to teach other people how to lead mindfulness in a way that fit the situation.
It wasn't just one class, anyway.
So I had some things that I was shy about too, but I had a feeling it would really help the world, and I had that fear like she did.
Who am I to bring superheroes to therapy?
Who am I to invent mindfulness classes?
Who am I to fill in the blank?
What is it for you?
Who am I to do that?
So it's a question of courage.
But anyway, in this conversation, Janina and I made a pact.
We agreed that she would bring superheroes to therapy, and I would do these experiments with mindfulness training and offerings, and we'd support each other.
And it actually worked.
It actually worked.
Or maybe it was one of many factors that helped those conversations grow.
I did those things, and they were reasonably successful at Mindfulness Northwest.
They served and helped a lot of people, I think.
And Janina is now actively engaging in superhero therapy.
That's her thing.
She's written 10 books on superhero therapy.
Here are a few of the titles.
Star Wars Psychology: The Dark Side of the Mind.
Game of Thrones Psychology: The Mind is Dark and Full of Terrors.
Doctor Who Psychology: A Madman with a Box.
Supernatural Psychology: Roads Less Traveled.
Wonder Woman Psychology: Lassoing the Truth.
Harry Potter Therapy: An Unauthorized Self-Help Book from the Restricted Section.
And Star Trek Psychology: The Mental Frontier.
Janina now gives keynote addresses at both comics conventions and psychology conventions.
Plus she met her soulmate and they got married in a Harry Potter wedding.
There's great wedding pictures of them casting spells on each other with their wands and dressed the right way.
So Janine is a real superhero to me.
We tried to keep in touch after this moving connection and these supportive courage conversations that did help us both, but you know how that goes.
The monthly conversation turns into every couple of months and then you forget.
But when she popped up in my inbox last week, I really paid notice.
She was reaching out to all of her American friends, maybe friends all over the world, I'm not sure, and asking us to join her in a time of practice to send loving-kindness and compassion to Ukraine.
I'm pretty resistant to any new thing showing up in my inbox, but this I knew I had to do, so I made it a priority and I went online and joined her and the others.
What I noticed was how hard it was to be on that call and practice for the Ukraine, hard and also good.

It was really hard to open the heart a little more to the suffering that must be there, knowing that I can only imagine, not experiencing that directly, and realizing I'd been avoiding feeling it, avoiding tuning in.
I tried not to read the news articles much beyond the headlines during the run-up to the invasion, right?
Like, oh, this isn't going to happen.
Maybe the whole world had some denial.
Just the utter strangeness of this: how could this kind of thing be happening in the 21st century, right?
Impossible.
I thought we were past that as a species, which is, of course, not the actual conversation of what's happening now.
So it was hard to be on that call and to open more to the suffering, but it was beautiful, too.
Janina led us with heart and grace and tears, and we held the suffering in our hearts and sent love, sent kindness, and sent compassion to Ukraine.
And maybe it really helps, maybe it somehow brought a little bit of ease on that particular day to a family that was trying to pack up and flee to Poland.
I don't know.
I really don't know.
But Janina felt it did.
So how could I not agree with her and bring my heart as fully as I could?
Because here's another whole area where we just don't know, do we?
Maybe we think we do know one way or the other, but I'm not so sure.
I do love science.
I love the scientific process and understanding.
I love that the wisdom teachings of Buddhism also shine a light on not knowing.
But the knowing of science and the not knowing of Buddhism seem like they line up most of the time.

It's been so powerful to me to be, in my own little way, a part of the conversation between science and Buddhism, or a westernized mindset and Buddhism from East Asia, doing the whole mindfulness thing and doing this thing here together with you.
We're not really doing this like Japanese people, even though we have some of the get-up.
We're translating and adapting, and we can't help but bring it into our worldview.
A lot of the core concepts and practices just flow easily from one world to the other, it seems.
Accepting and understanding stress, another word for suffering.
Learning that we can shift the way we relate and have conversation with everything.
That there's no intrinsic result from any extrinsic factor.
That it's all on how we relate to it and how we understand it, and it's affected by our conditioning.
Of course, we can't control the darn thing, but there's more freedom and more fluidity in everything than we think.
And of course, the healing, the unbelievable healing power of sitting still, just being in our breathing, just being.
I do often marvel at that anew, and it's something I keep repeating out loud, I think: we could never have thought of this, right?
We would never have imagined that it would be not only a good idea, but transformational and deeply important to rent a church hall and sit around for three days doing nothing.
It's amazing.
It's so good.
And what a great antidote that is to multitasking in this crazy, overly busy world, a big counterweight.
Chop wood, carry water.
When eating, just eat.
When walking, just walk.
So why not, when writing an email, just write that one email?
What's the difference?
It's so applicable.
So many Buddhist ideas and practices just flow freely and easily into our cultural frame, using some degree of Buddhist language or just using ordinary American language or psychology language.
It's just language.
And yet some aspects are a little more challenging, maybe more religious, maybe more esoteric.
Again, just words, but words that point to the territory.
Buddhism suggests, like pretty much every other world religion, that there are unseen forces at play here and that the mind is not the kind of mind that we think of that just thinks thoughts.
So there I was sitting in Zoom with Janina and friends doing loving-kindness and sending the good energy to Ukraine.
Does that help?
Does that work?
Does that even make sense?
It's a more difficult fit into our conceptual, scientific Western frame.
It's hard not to put quotation marks around this idea in Buddhism of merit, quotation marks or footnotes or something.
It's hard to just take it straight.
Is there really an unseen good energy that we generate when we practice?
And then we can direct it to someone.
And could it be that directing it to someone is not just a nice thing to do, but a tremendously enormous act of generosity, like the most important thing you could actually do?
This is how the teachings seem to go.

So we re-understand our little ceremonies after sitting, our services, in this way, not just as a little cultural thing that we aren't quite confident letting go of yet, but actually as the important part.
Now we've generated merit.
Let's give it away.
This is huge.
Sending it to honored bodhisattvas, to hungry ghosts, to the planet, to the people in Ukraine and Russia.
There's some fringy science that lines up, but it probably will always remain on the fringe.
Sometimes it pops up in mainstream settings, so it's interesting: the science of one person thinking something and somebody else being affected in some way.
Sometimes they throw in the term quantum mechanics, but I suspect every time somebody says quantum mechanics, they don't really know what that is.
I don't really know the physics.
Probably only a handful of people in the world really do, but it sounds good.
It's from physics.
So I don't know if merit's a real thing, but maybe our hearts know.
And maybe being in conversation with suffering is the most important thing we can be doing, should be doing, are doing.
And maybe we don't need to worry about it so much, just practice, just offer.
So let's offer whatever merit comes from this practice, these talks, this retreat, whatever momentum and energy we've built up by having practice periods every year and wonderful shusos every year.
Why don't we offer that to the suffering world, especially to everyone who's suffering in Ukraine and in Russia too.
Of course, it's not a good guy, bad guy story anyway.
It's not just like the superhero stories.
It's a complex, dynamic, difficult situation for everybody involved, with so much suffering.
Russian families are coping with a crashing economy, rising prices.

I read somewhere black bread has risen from two rubles a loaf to 11, and that Russian people are encouraging each other to buy consumer goods and hide them in the attic somewhere, because hopefully they'll be able to sell them later, since their cash will likely be worth nothing soon.
And meanwhile, in the Ukraine, a million people now have left, mostly through Poland, but almost all women and children and older men.
The government of Ukraine has banned men between the ages of 18 and 60 from leaving the country.
They can stay and fight.
There's a lot there, and I'm sure I only know just the very tip of the iceberg.
Always more than what we think, for sure.
More suffering, more love, more courage, more confusion than we can know.
And so, usually our minds want to have a narrow view, write a simple story, and so it's great that we hung out in the Diamond Sutra so long, and I know some of us didn't.
It's hard to speak up when everyone else is like, oh, this sutra is so cool, and you are like, are we done yet?
Let me go back to normal stuff.
It's a weird way of speaking, the Diamond Sutra, isn't it?
It's a kind of yoga for the mind that basically involves asanas that your body can't do.
Very carefully described.
It's like someone took that giant BKS Iyengar book and reinvented it all in things that are impossible.
It's okay to do this.
But I do want to bring us back to it just briefly.
As you, Hannah, mentioned this too, I mostly felt a little bit at sea this time around.
I've studied the Diamond Sutra many times, and this time it wasn't really connecting for me either, for the most part.
That's okay.
But for some reason, in verse 13, which the scholars think is a bit of a pivot point in the history of the text, something opened up for me.

That's the one where Buddha finally tells Subhuti what the name of the sutra is, and then pulls out all the stops yet again, trying to explain to Subhuti how incredible, how merit-producing, and how rich it is to even just recite or have a feeling for a couple of lines, a four-line gatha, they keep saying, how important and powerful that is.

So I want to share with you Thich Nhat Hanh's comment after verse 13, where he encouraged us not to get too caught up in all the metaphors, sands of Ganges and chillicosms and this and that, but to realize how radically the conversation we're having with the world will change if we get out of our own way, if we get out of the way of life.
So here's how he says it.
*If someone were to grind the 3000 chillicosms into dust, these particles of dust would be very, very many.
We should look deeply into the concepts like many, and chillicosms with the eye of transcendent understanding if we want to avoid being caught up by these concepts.
The same is true of concepts like dust, 32 marks.
Although such words are used, we should not be caught by them.

If someone were to accept, practice, and explain these teachings, even only a verse of four lines, the happiness resulted would be far greater than the happiness that would result from any other virtuous act.
Because the practice of non-attainment, as it is taught in the Sutra, can liberate us completely from wrong views.
The happiness that results from this practice is far greater than any other kind of happiness.
The practice of non-attachment, non-attainment, non-self, as it is taught in the Sutra, can liberate us completely from wrong views, and the happiness that results is huge.*
He goes on to say, and this is important to us as bodhisattvas:
*Virtuous acts that are still based on the ground of self, person, living being, and lifespan may bring some happiness, may bring some happiness.
But compared to the happiness of true liberation, it's still quite small.
When a person is cut free, is free from wrong views, his or her actions will greatly benefit the world.
The practice of the diamond that cuts through illusion is thus the basis for all meaningful action.*
So the Diamond Sutra makes huge claims, so of course in the commentary Thich Nhat Hanh makes huge claims, that there is this sea change, right, this huge difference.
If the basis is me, or the basis is bigger, if the basis is the conversation itself, the basis is freedom, is letting go, is courage.
But it's courage that doesn't need somebody to be courageous in the middle of it.
It's just courage.
Then the actions are just so much more beneficial, so much more helpful, and I assume the merit we send is so much more powerful.
How do we do this?
Well, [unclear: "the Catholic"] did a good, nice job yesterday reminding us: no clue.
We don't know.
But we do know.
We do know how to practice.
We do know how to continue this long, careful conversation, where we notice suffering, we notice constriction, we notice pulling away from fear and pain, and we come back.
We come back.
And Zazen is such a wonderful training ground for that.
What else are we doing in Zazen?

Sometimes it seems low-key, we're just sitting there, but actually, if we're paying attention, we're doing this conversation with our experience, moment to moment, noticing everything that happens and coming back.
And that instant of return is an instant of this freedom, this freedom from wrong views.
Noticing our narrowness, we come back to the conversation with more heart.
And naturally, there's more courage.
We don't make it.
Naturally, there's more courage.
We come back to the soft soil, where these wisdom teachings can take root.
And maybe you've got to plant the darn seeds a lot of times.

It's hard to know, if you are having trouble relating to stuff like the Diamond Sutra, whether that means you should move on to stuff you relate to, or you should basically read it every day for the rest of your life.
It's hard to know.
What should you do as a servant of the world?
A world that does have this everyday, describable, measurable reality, it seems, and a world with magic, a world of superheroes, a world with merit we can send to suffering beings everywhere.
How could it just be one or the other?
It's not possible.

So I guess all that's to say, or some attempt at saying, I was feeling uncomfortable with the conversation I was having when I wrote this, so I hope it was useful in this conversation, because that's when it matters.
All this to say, let's just keep having the conversation.
Conversation of practice, of love, of community, of service, of not knowing, and little by little, inevitably, our fixed views will soften.
It seems to just happen, and we won't believe them quite as much.
So, lastly, it seems appropriate, this being the last talk of the practice period, to appreciate anew the last verse of the Diamond Sutra.
Probably, as I mentioned, scholars do say that the last verses were added on later.
This stuff was recited and recopied and recited and recopied, and there was no master copy on the internet, so things could get added over time.
So, maybe so.

The conceit that this really happened as a real conversation between Sabuddhi and the Buddha is also true, and it's also true this was written down hundreds of years after the Buddha wasn't walking around in the Dharmakaya human body, and other people wrote it.
But whoever wrote it, I feel like they offered us this little gift at the end.
It's like, well, if you're all bent up and twisted into knots like a pretzel from the conceptual damage the Diamond Sutra Yoga has done to your mind, we now will liberate you again.
Here's the antidote, this beautiful little poem.
Here's Mu Soeng's translation.
*So you should view all of the feeling worlds, fleeting worlds, sorry.
So you should view all of the fleeting worlds.
A star at dawn, a bubble in the stream, a flash of lightning, and a summer cloud, a flickering lamp, a phantom, and a dream.
So you should view all the fleeting worlds.
A star at dawn, a bubble in the stream, a flash of lightning, and a summer cloud, a flickering lamp, a phantom, and a dream.*
It's such a relief when we can feel that part of it too.
It's not all as solid and monolithic as we think it is.
And there's nothing to hold on to in the conversation.
And may all of us and everyone else in the world bring forth the courage we need, the love we need.
Thanks very much.
Give Chris your bell there.
So what it is is [unclear: "wondering at the end of each of the vowel lines and then in a roll down"].
*The beings are numerous, I better save them.*

verbatim.text: Good morning everybody. I feel not as connected to you guys this retreat. So anyway, I've been thinking about you. The Dokusan room turns out doesn't really have Wi-Fi that so it's hard to connect in Dokusan. So what can you do? So as earlier, can you hear me okay like this? Okay. All right. You guys can hear? Okay. I was appreciating earlier, I was looking at the job sheet, you know, make a little job sheet who does what job.
